This article is about the physical quantity. For other uses, see Kinetic.
Common symbolsKE, Ek

Kinetic energy (from the Greek kinesis, meaning "motion") is the form of energy that an object possesses due to its motion.[1] The kinetic energy of an object equals the work needed to accelerate it from rest to its stated velocity.

In classical mechanics, kinetic energy depends on the mass and the velocity of the object, as described in the kinetic energy article.

[edit]Newtonian kinetic energy

The kinetic energy of a moving object increases with the square of its velocity and in direct proportion to its mass.

{\displaystyle E_{k}={\frac {1}{2}}mv^{2}}

The term was introduced in 1829 by Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis, who also described the associated work.

The work–energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.[2]

For a rotating rigid body, the rotational kinetic energy is , where I is the moment of inertia.

Work–energy theorem

Integrating Newton's second law along a path converts the net force into a change in kinetic energy.

Applying the work–energy theorem to a falling object shows that gravity produces an increase in kinetic energy.

Applications

Braking converts the kinetic energy of a vehicle into thermal energy through friction.

History

The concept developed from the work of Gottfried Leibniz, who described the vis viva in 1686 and argued that it is conserved.
